description: Welcome to our team's page for the 2026 Space Apps Challenge! We're diving into NASA's microgravity combustion research to craft interactive AI tools that help scientists analyze fire safety data for lunar and Martian missions.
summary: FLAMEVERSE is an interactive, Superintelligence-powered spacecraft fire safety Command Center built for the Flame in Freefall challenge. We developed IGNIS-SI, a domain-grounded Space Fire Superintelligence backed by live queries to the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Combustion Science API (24 investigations), the NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) API, A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015), historical mission mishap archives (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, and the 1997 Mir Fire), and NASA Earth spin-offs (Fireman's Air Tanks). Instead of forcing researchers to dig through scattered PDFs, FLAMEVERSE dynamically summarizes, ranks, simulates, and interprets fire prevention, detection, suppression, and physics findings across Earth (1G), Moon (0.16G), Mars (0.38G), and microgravity (0G). By comparing high-oxygen exploration habitats (such as Moon Base 30% O2 at ≤10.2 psi vs. Earth 21% O2 at 14.7 psi) and exposing partial-gravity evidence gaps prior to LUCI/FM2, FLAMEVERSE helps protect future Artemis crews and advances terrestrial fire safety.
details:
What does it do & how does it work?

IGNIS-SI (Superintelligence Core): Accepts natural-language questions (or 1-click incident feeds), performs live keyword-routed lookups against psi.nasa.gov and ntrs.nasa.gov, and uses Google Gemini (@google/genai) with curated NASA baselines to return cited, confidence-scored answers with clickable PSI/NTRS links.

Dynamic Ranking & Summary Dashboards: Continuously scores and ranks NASA PSI investigations (#1–#5 in the Command Center + full matrix in the Looker Analytics Hub) as users adjust Gravity, Oxygen (14–100%), Pressure (kPa/psi), Airflow (0–1.2 m/s), Material, and Ignition Source, alongside 4-pillar summaries (Prevention, Detection, Suppression, Fundamental).

Interactive Fire Lab & Historical Incident Simulator: Renders real-time 1G buoyant vs. 0G spherical flame behavior, thermal rise curves, O2 × Airflow risk heatmaps, and reconstructs Apollo 1 (1967), Apollo 13 (1970), and Mir (1997) to feed incident-specific lessons straight into IGNIS-SI.

Benefits: Replaces hours of manual literature search with instant, traceable NASA citations; links physics simulation directly to flight evidence; exports CSV telemetry, AI flight test proposals (SOFIE / LUCI / FM2), and .txt Mission Safety Dossiers.

Intended Impact: Helps Artemis/Mars mission designers evaluate enriched-oxygen habitat flammability safely, accelerates research into the zero-data partial-gravity gap (0.16G / 0.38G), and highlights NASA-to-Earth safety transfers like composite firefighter SCBA tanks and water-mist extinguishers.

Tools, Languages & Stack Used:

Languages & Frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, HTML5 Canvas, Vite 8, Node.js + Express (tsx).

AI & Analytics: Google Gemini API (@google/genai), Looker Analytics Hub UI, Google AI Studio(for building parts of the SL/ML into the project).

Cloud & DevOps: Google Cloud, Google Cloud Run (Dockerized deployment at flameverse.earth), GitHub, GoDaddy/porkbun DNS/SSL.

Data Sources: Live NASA PSI API (psi.nasa.gov), NASA NTRS API (ntrs.nasa.gov), 2015 ISS Combustion Researcher's Guide, Apollo 1 & 13 Archives, Mir 1997 Archive, and NASA Spinoff (Fireman's Air Tanks).

How is it creative? Rather than a static chatbot or chart dashboard, FLAMEVERSE unifies a Command Center Superintelligence (IGNIS-SI), live dual-NASA APIs, Earth-vs-Space Fire Twin visual simulation, and clickable historical disaster reconstruction (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir '97) into one connected mission-control loop.

Factors Considered: Eliminating hallucinated science via strict PSI/NTRS provenance and live verified URLs; accurately expressing Moon Base (30% O2, ≤10.2 psi) vs. Earth (21% O2, 14.7 psi) partial-pressure flammability; clearly flagging unvalidated partial-gravity regimes (0 lunar/Martian datasets in PSI); and graceful local PSI cache fallbacks.
